title: Memorizing definitions instead of applying them
description: You can recite the theory perfectly but freeze when the scenario changes the shape of the question. Examiners repeatedly note that numerical work is answered reasonably well while theory applied to the case scores poorly — the gap is not what you know, it is whether you can use it.
why: Study time goes into textbooks and flashcards, not into explaining concepts back in your own words or linking them to real situations. In the exam, the case never mirrors the textbook example, so memorized paragraphs have nowhere to land.
damage: Written answers stay textbook-generic and earn knowledge-level marks at best; application and analysis marks are lost entirely. Across sessions this pattern is the single biggest drag on theory questions.
weak: A question asks for the effect of a government import-tax waiver on a car assembler's strategy. The answer reproduces the textbook PESTEL list — Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental — with a one-line generic definition under each, and never mentions the tax waiver or the assembler.
strong: The answer picks the two or three factors the waiver actually moves (economic: lower landed cost of kits; legal/political: policy credibility and reversal risk), explains each in one or two sentences tied to the assembler, and ignores the factors that do not matter here.
checklist: For every model you revise, rehearse explaining it in two sentences without the book open
Practise each theory on at least one invented scenario before the exam
In the answer, forbid yourself from writing any sentence that could appear in another company's answer
Read one paraphrased examiner observation per week and ask: would my answer have avoided this?
practice: Pick any two frameworks from your syllabus. For each, write a 150-word explanation of how it would apply to a company facing a sudden currency devaluation — no textbook copying allowed.

title: Answering without the case facts
description: The answer reads like a model answer written for a different company. Case-specific numbers, names, dates, thresholds and product details are never used, so the marker cannot tell whether you read the scenario at all.
why: Skimming the case to 'save time' means key figures — cut-offs, contract sizes, capacity limits, customer profiles — never enter working memory. Candidates then fall back on generic knowledge they are comfortable with.
damage: Every application mark in a constructed-response question depends on using the given facts; generic answers miss them all. Examiners also note outright wrong conclusions when the ignored facts would have changed the answer (wrong quadrant, wrong segment, wrong product).
weak: Asked whether three market segments suit a premium menswear brand for ages 18–40, the answer evaluates each segment on general appeal — 'large market, growing demand' — and recommends entering all three, ignoring the facts that the segments are cost-conscious and outside the target age.
strong: The answer first tests each segment against the brand's stated positioning and the 18–40 age band, notes that none of the three fits (cost-conscious buyers are the wrong fit), and discusses that mismatch explicitly instead of recommending entry.
checklist: Underline or list every number and named fact in the case before you start writing
Check: does my answer mention at least three case-specific facts? If not, rework it
For classification tasks (segments, quadrants, stages), test each item against the stated criteria before judging it
If a case fact seems irrelevant, assume you have missed its use — re-read the requirement
practice: Take one past case question. List every fact given, then mark which of your draft answer's points used each fact. Rewrite any point that used none.

title: Listing without analysis
description: Factors, controls, stages or steps are named and then left to stand alone — no discussion, no 'so what', no reasoning linking them to the decision. Examiners keep saying the same thing: identification earns little without the discussion that follows.
why: Listing feels productive and fills the page, so candidates stop there. The habit comes from memorization-heavy revision: names are easy to recall, but the reasoning behind them was never practised.
damage: Analysis marks are the middle layer of the mark scheme and are the most commonly missed. A full list with zero discussion routinely halves the marks available on a 6–8 mark question.
weak: A SWOT question gets four bullet lists — strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats — copied from the scenario, with no sentence explaining why any factor matters or what the company should do about it.
strong: After listing the factors, each gets one line of discussion: 'The new plant is a strength because it cuts the bottleneck that caused last year's lost orders; its threat is the pending regulation that could close that line — so the priority is…'.
checklist: After every named item, force one sentence starting 'This matters because…'
Re-read the command word: 'discuss', 'analyze' and 'explain' all demand reasoning, not names
Budget answer lines roughly equally between naming and discussing
Before submitting, count named items vs discussed items — they should roughly match
practice: Take a past SWOT or PESTEL answer you wrote (or sketch one). Add a two-line discussion under every factor. Time yourself: keep each to two lines.

title: Recommendations with no justification
description: The answer reaches a recommendation — hedge, don't hedge, enter the segment, disclose the breach — but never says why it wins over the alternatives. Examiners withhold the evaluation marks because the decision is a verdict with no reasoning.
why: Candidates do the analysis, feel the answer is 'obvious', and skip writing the reasoning down. Often only one option was really worked through, so there is nothing to weigh in the conclusion.
damage: Evaluation-level questions are where the paper's top marks live (Section B case questions up to 15 marks). An unjustified recommendation typically scores the analysis and loses the evaluation band — often 30–40% of the question's marks.
weak: After comparing three investment options, the answer ends: 'Therefore the company should choose Option B.' — no weighing of the downsides, no explanation of what the alternatives lose on.
strong: The answer ends: 'Option B is recommended because it preserves liquidity while meeting the capacity need; Option A fails on the payback requirement and Option C locks the company into a six-year contract it may not need. The main risk is…'
checklist: End every case question with a conclusion that references at least two alternatives
Use 'because' twice in every recommendation sentence
Check the requirement: if it says 'recommend and justify', the justification is half the marks
Acknowledge the main counterargument or downside, then say why it is outweighed
practice: Take a past case question with multiple options. Write the recommendation first, then spend five minutes listing every reason against it. Rewrite the conclusion using those reasons as the justification.

title: Misreading the requirement and command words
description: The answer is technically competent but aimed at the wrong target: the wrong period (monthly instead of cumulative), the wrong count (three factors listed instead of five), the wrong depth ('identify' done to 'discuss' standard or vice versa). Examiners call these misdirected answers — marks lost without any knowledge gap.
why: Skimming the requirement under time pressure, or pattern-matching to a question practised before instead of reading the one on the page. Multi-part questions get answered as one blob.
damage: Zero or partial credit on a question the candidate could have answered. These are the most painful lost marks because no extra studying would have saved them — only reading would.
weak: The requirement asks for a cumulative nine-month net cash inflow/(outflow) budget. The answer presents neat monthly budgets — correct arithmetic, wrong deliverable.
strong: Before writing, the candidate circles 'cumulative nine-month' and 'net cash inflow/(outflow)' in the requirement, sets up one cumulative column for nine months, and checks each part's output against the exact words of its requirement.
checklist: Read every requirement twice; underline the command word and the deliverable
Translate the requirement into one sentence: 'They want X, in Y format, for Z period'
Check each part of multi-part questions is answered separately and labelled
In the last two minutes, re-check deliverables against the requirement wording, not your memory
practice: Take five past-paper requirements. For each, write only: command word, deliverable, period/format, marks. Compare with the actual question afterwards.

title: No plan, no clock — time wasted where marks aren't
description: Long generic passages are written where two scenario-specific lines were needed; easy marks at the end go unattempted. Examiners explicitly ask for better exam technique: plan answers and address every part of each question.
why: Writing starts before thinking. The comfortable parts of a question get overwritten while the awkward parts get avoided, and nobody allocates minutes to marks — roughly 1.8 minutes per mark on this paper.
damage: A question worth 15 marks with 10 minutes spent on a 4-mark part starves the remaining parts. Entire requirements go unanswered while over-answered parts earn no more than their capped marks.
weak: A 4-mark 'criticize the model' part gets a full page of textbook criticism while the 8-mark application part that follows gets three rushed lines.
strong: The candidate marks each requirement with its marks, jots a 60-second bullet plan per part, writes in mark order (heavy parts first if needed), and stops a part when its minutes are up.
checklist: Allocate minutes to marks before writing: 100 marks ÷ 180 minutes ≈ 1.8 minutes per mark
Spend 60–90 seconds planning each part: bullets, not prose, first
Stop writing a part when its time is up — capped marks mean extra lines earn nothing
Attempt every part; an outline answer to the last part beats a perfect answer to the first
practice: Do a timed 15-mark case question: 27 minutes on the clock, plan on scrap first. Afterward, mark which parts were over- or under-written and by how much.

title: Generic conclusions the marker can't reward
description: The conclusion could be pasted onto any company's answer: 'higher profits', 'better decisions', 'the environment is helped'. Examiners reward conclusions that follow from the case's own numbers and facts — generics signal the analysis never really happened.
why: Conclusions get written last, in a hurry, from habit rather than from the workings above them. Candidates also fear committing to a specific claim in case it is wrong.
damage: The final 2–4 marks of case questions are conclusion marks; generic ones earn none. Worse, a vague conclusion can undermine an otherwise decent analysis.
weak: After a working-capital computation, the conclusion reads: 'The new technology will increase profit and revenue for the company.' — true of almost anything, proven by nothing above it.
strong: The conclusion reads: 'Because the app answers the two concerns customers actually raise — battery range and charging time — it should raise EV adoption among the company's existing SUV buyers; the cash effect is a Rs 40m first-year contribution per the workings above.'
checklist: Forbid conclusions that could fit another company
Reference at least one computed figure or named case fact in every conclusion
Write the conclusion immediately after the workings, while the numbers are in front of you
Ask: 'which line of my workings proves this sentence?' — if none, rewrite it
practice: Re-read three of your old conclusions (or invent three generic ones). Rewrite each so it only fits the specific company and uses one figure from the workings.

title: Dropping facts into the wrong model step
description: Model steps are used as loose decoration instead of a sequence: ethical-reasoning steps mixed together, PESTEL factors filed under the wrong letter, strategy recommendations placed before the analysis that supports them. The logic breaks even when the individual points are right.
why: The model was memorized as a list of headings, not learned as a thinking sequence. Under pressure, everything recalled gets written under the nearest heading.
damage: Examiners report this as 'poor structure' and withhold analysis marks because the reasoning cannot be followed — the points exist but the argument doesn't.
weak: A seven-step ethical decision model gets used as three headings; 'alternative courses of action' appear under 'identify the ethical issue', and the final recommendation appears halfway through the analysis.
strong: Each model step is a headed section in order: issue → stakeholders → alternatives → norms and principles → decision → justification. Points that belong to step 4 are moved out of step 2 before submission.
checklist: Learn models as sequences ('first this, then this'), not as word lists
Write each step as a heading and police your points into the right one
In the final check, re-read headings only — the story should make sense from headings alone
For PESTEL/SWOT, re-test each factor against its letter before moving on
practice: Take a model you know (PESTEL, SWOT, an ethics model). Write one question's worth of points, deliberately shuffle them, then re-sort them into the right steps as a sorting drill.

title: Skipping parts — or whole questions — entirely
description: Parts (b) and (c) go unattempted; sometimes a whole question is left blank. Examiners link this to selective preparation — entire syllabus areas were never studied — and to candidates who answer what they know instead of what is asked.
why: Study skips the 'hard' or 'boring' areas (statistics, working capital, sustainability frameworks); in the exam, anything outside the comfort zone is abandoned instead of attempted for partial marks.
damage: Unattempted parts score zero by definition. On this paper, even a basic attempt at every part routinely earns more than perfect answers to half the paper.
weak: Question 5 has three parts; the candidate answers (a) well and leaves (b) and (c) blank because they involve a model never revised.
strong: The candidate writes a structured attempt at all three parts: part (b) gets a clear statement of the model's steps applied to the case facts, earning method marks even where the numbers are shaky.
checklist: Prepare all syllabus areas — selective study leaves whole questions unattempted
In the exam, never leave a part blank: write the setup, the formula, or the first steps for method marks
If stuck, attempt the requirement at a lower depth ('identify' even if you can't 'evaluate')
Track your coverage in revision: every grid area needs at least one timed attempt
practice: Pick your least favourite grid area. Attempt one past question from it in 20 minutes, aiming only for method and structure marks — no perfection allowed.

title: Misreading the given numbers
description: The method is right but the inputs are wrong: inflation applied from year 2 instead of year 1, a cum-dividend price used as ex-dividend, monthly figures treated as annual, bid and ask rates confused, wrong tax treatment on a dividend. These are reading errors that corrupt correct technique.
why: Numbers are lifted from the case without checking what they represent — the qualifier words (cum, ex, per month, from year 1, at premium) get skipped. No sanity check is run on the result.
damage: One wrong input poisons every figure downstream — revenue, tax, WACC, NPV — and the final recommendation built on them. Examiners see this across sessions as the most frequent source of lost numerical marks.
weak: A Rs 78 share price is used directly in the dividend-growth cost-of-equity calculation, ignoring the stated Rs 8 dividend — so the Rs 70 ex-dividend price is never derived and equity value and cost of equity are both overstated.
strong: The candidate lists each given figure with its qualifier before calculating: 'Rs 78 cum-dividend → ex-div = Rs 70', 'inflation from year 1, compounded yearly', 'monthly visitors × 12'. A final glance asks: does this number make sense?
checklist: Copy every given number with its qualifier word (cum/ex, per month/per year, from year 1)
Sanity-check results against basics: cost of equity should not fall below the risk-free rate
Re-read the case line by line after finishing the workings — did every number get used correctly?
For rates and prices, label each as bid/ask, deposit/borrowing, nominal/market before using it
practice: Re-do a past numerical question using only this rule: no number enters a formula until its qualifier is written next to it. Compare with your first attempt.

title: Treating sunk costs as decision-relevant
description: Money already spent — feasibility studies, past estimates, an option premium already paid — is folded into the new decision's cash flows. Examiners keep catching this, and one such error typically cascades through depreciation, residual values and the final recommendation.
why: It feels wrong to ignore money that was really spent, so candidates include it 'to be safe'. The decision-relevance test (does this cash flow change because of my decision?) is never applied.
damage: The investment figure, tax computations and NPV all shift; conclusions reverse on polluted numbers. Examiners treat it as an application failure even when the discounting technique is perfect.
weak: A Rs 15 million feasibility spend — already incurred — is included in the project's initial outflow, overstating the investment and corrupting the depreciation, residual-value and disposal figures that follow.
strong: Before building the cash flows, the candidate strikes through every already-incurred figure in the case and writes 'sunk — exclude' next to it; only future, decision-dependent cash flows enter the appraisal.
checklist: Ask for every figure: 'Would this cash flow change if we say no?' — if not, exclude it
Mark sunk items in the case (past spend, prior estimates, already-paid premiums) before you start
Remember: past revenues and costs from old estimates are sunk too, not just cash spent
Check your workings: no struck-through item should appear anywhere in them
practice: Take a past investment-appraisal question. List every figure and tag each 'sunk' or 'relevant' with a one-line reason before touching the numbers.

title: Confusing look-alike concepts
description: Strengths are listed as opportunities, fairness is discussed under rightness, restructuring is mixed with de-layering, resources with competencies. The question then gets an answer built on the wrong concept — confident, detailed, and wrong.
why: Pairs of terms are revised together without ever being contrasted. In the exam, the more familiar term gets used for both.
damage: Everything downstream of the confusion is marked wrong: factors in the wrong SWOT quadrant, the wrong ethical dimension analyzed, the wrong strategy recommended. Examiners note this year after year, especially in ethics and strategic-analysis questions.
weak: A Tucker five-question ethics answer discusses 'fairness' (equitable treatment of regulators, hospitals and patients) under the 'rightness' heading and vice versa, so neither dimension is actually addressed.
strong: The candidate writes the distinction first: 'Fairness = equitable treatment of affected parties; rightness = alignment with broader ethical and moral principles' — then answers each question under its own heading using that test.
checklist: Revise confusable pairs side by side: write the one-line difference for each
In the exam, state the distinction at the top of the answer before applying it
After writing, re-test: does every point sit under the heading it actually belongs to?
Flashcard the pairs (strengths/opportunities, fairness/rightness, resources/competencies) as two-sided comparisons
practice: List five concept pairs you personally confuse. For each, write the one-line test that separates them, then apply both to a one-paragraph scenario.

title: Echoing the question instead of answering it
description: The 'explanation' just restates the scenario's wording, or lists every principle when the question asked for the relevant ones. The marker sees recall of the question text, not understanding of it.
why: Blank-page panic: repeating the question feels like writing something relevant. In ethics questions, candidates dump all five principles hoping the right one is somewhere in the pile.
damage: Zero analysis marks — the answer adds nothing to the question. Dumping all principles wastes time and signals the candidate cannot select, which is itself what is being tested.
weak: Asked to identify the information-system type and explain it, the answer names the type correctly, then 'explains' it by copying the scenario's description of the system word for word.
strong: The answer names the system type, then explains in its own words what such a system does and why it fits this company's situation — using the scenario's facts as evidence, not as the explanation itself.
checklist: Never copy a scenario sentence into your answer as if it were analysis
In ethics questions, select the principles that fit the case — don't list all of them
Explain in your own words: if your sentence could be highlighted in the question, rewrite it
Relevance first, completeness second — the examiner tests selection, not memory
practice: Take a past scenario question you answered by echoing. Highlight every sentence that repeats the question's wording, then rewrite the answer without those sentences.

title: Deciding before analyzing
description: The answer picks a winner early — the cheapest option, the obvious hedge, the attractive-looking strategy — and the 'analysis' just dresses up that choice. Examiners catch this when the strategy contradicts the scenario (prices expected to rise yet futures recommended) or when only one option is really worked through.
why: Anchoring: the first plausible answer feels right, and the rest of the answer is built to defend it. Time pressure makes working through all options feel like a luxury.
damage: When the scenario points the other way, the whole evaluation band is lost. Even when the choice happens to be right, the missing comparison of alternatives costs the justification marks.
weak: With the scenario clearly indicating rising prices, the answer recommends futures as the best hedging strategy — the analysis then justifies futures without ever testing 'no hedging' against the price direction.
strong: The answer works through each strategy against the expected price movement and the hedger's position, notes that rising prices make no hedging optimal, and only then recommends — with the comparison as the justification.
checklist: Work through every option before writing any recommendation
Test your instinct against the scenario's direction (price trends, risk appetite, constraints)
If the 'obvious' choice wins, say explicitly which alternatives lost and why
Include the 'do nothing' option in every hedge/investment evaluation
practice: Take a past hedging or investment question. Deliberately argue for the option you would not choose first, then decide — and check whether your recommendation changes.
